title: Christian funerals (CCC 1680–1690)
hookLine: the Church accompanies the dead with hope and commends them to God

cards: The coffin comes in at the back of the church, and the priest meets it at the door. He sprinkles it with water, the way water was poured on this person at baptism, long ago, maybe in this same building.
A white cloth is spread over the wood; nobody can tell whether the one inside was rich or poor. The family walks behind, eyes down. By the altar burns the candle that was lit at Easter.

teach.h: DEATH IN THE LIGHT OF THE RESURRECTION.
teach.b: The Catechism begins with hope. For a Christian, death is seen in the light of Christ's death and resurrection.
Jesus tells Martha, in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "I am the resurrection and the life: he that believeth in me, although he be dead, shall live." That's the key the whole funeral is played in.
It doesn't give the dead a sacrament, the Catechism says. It expresses the Church's communion with them, gathers the living, and proclaims eternal life. Then the shape of the rite.
First, the greeting. In the rite, the community welcomes the person one last time, at the door, as it once did at baptism, and speaks words of comfort and hope to the family.
Second, the word. Scripture is read, even in grief, because the Church holds that God's word speaks into death too. Wisdom, in the Douay-Rheims: "the souls of the just are in the hand of God."
Third, the Eucharist. The Church offers the Mass for the one who has died; Catholics believe this prayer helps them, and that the bond between the living and the dead isn't broken.

Fourth, the farewell. The Church commends the person to God: the community's last goodbye before the body goes to the grave. A commendation is a handing over: here is someone we loved; we place them in your hands.
Today also closes Part Two, How we celebrate, which ran from the liturgy and the sacraments to sacramentals, devotions and this farewell: from the font to the grave.

how: A Catholic funeral usually includes a vigil or wake, a funeral Mass with the coffin received at the church door and covered with a white pall, and a final commendation before burial, with prayers at the graveside.

o: a private family ritual with no church role
a sacrament that forgives the sins of the dead
a farewell that hands the dead to God, in hope

games.q: the funeral Mass is ending. the priest stands by the coffin with the family. what does the rite do now?
o: a long speech summing up the life.
the farewell: the Church commends the person to God.
games.why: the rite ends with the final commendation, the Church's last farewell, handing the person over to God.

practice: Remember one funeral you've been to, the music, the faces, the moment the coffin left, and bring back the person; say their name quietly.
If you pray, commend them to God, in silence or with words of the Church you already know; if you don't, remember them with gratitude.
And if grief has taken you somewhere dark, or you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: Christian funerals. The Church meets the dead at the door, reads the word, offers the Eucharist, and, at the farewell, commends them to God, in the hope of the resurrection. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: an entrusting, a handing over into someone's care.

carryVoice: Your line: commended to God. A handing over, made in hope of resurrection. Until tomorrow.
